comment: Charging for reviewing tree work seems reasonable. I'm less clear why every standalone grading application would have one flat fee.
I do landscape work. Non-refundable at the application stage worries me when a homeowner is still trying to find out what can be permitted. Need to see the actual schedule.
Ravines are something I come to enjoy, even though I don't own land beside one. I'm comfortable with applicants contributing to the cost of reviewing work there.
fee structure yes, maybe. voting on the price without seeing it? cant really do that
Per tree could add up for someone with several trees to deal with. That is my concern, rather than treating grading as the same thing.
Complex jobs and simple jobs shouldn't automatically have the same application charge. The complexity part makes sense from a quoting perspective, provided people can work out which category applies.
The tree part has a rationale. Neither for nor against the flat grading fee from this summary.
My yard already feels like paperwork with a fence around it. I don't want another application fee.
A fee for reviewing changes in a ravine area seems fair. Please don't present payment as permission to damage whatever you like.
Is the tree count the number in the application? Would like a worked example before deciding.
I pass ravine areas regularly but have no experience applying for this. Leaving the grading question open.
Flat fee is easy to explain to a client. Whether it's fair is a different question and I haven't got the figures.
Fine with application review having a cost. A clear invoice matters more to me than another long explanation of the bylaw.
I'd rather more of this review be funded generally. Ravines have a public value too; the applicant isn't the only person with a stake in how they're managed.
Which fees, and how much? I can see the reference to the appendices but the notice alone isn't enough for my vote.
Services need funding. I lean toward the proposed package on that basis, though I'd still want to go through the rates before treating this as final approval.
I work in a small business and need predictable costs. I'm against approving a whole bundle of charges together when I can't assess them individually here.
not a yes or a no from me. A package this broad could contain things I'd vote differently on
Hard to connect this notice to what I actually use when visiting. The appendix is doing a lot of work.
Another fee discussion. My patience for paying at every turn has run out.
I favour using user fees as part of service funding, so I'm supportive of considering this package. That doesn't tell me every proposed rate is right; those still deserve scrutiny.
Would need to sit down with A and B and check what's relevant to our work. No idea yet what the net effect would be.
Affordability is my sticking point. I don't favour the package as presented without a clearer explanation of who would have difficulty paying.
Keeping services running matters to me. Tentative yes to the package, with the rates needing a proper explanation.
Proposed, not final. Are people reading this as the actual adopted budget? I haven't seen enough here to choose a side.
Too broad for a strong view.
I don't expect every service to be free. A published fee schedule is useful, and overall I'm open to this approach.
A short before-and-after table would help. I dislike being asked to approve the principle first and chase down what it costs later.
Funding and access both count. I can't weigh them for this particular package from the notice text.
I started looking for one amount and realised this is an entire package. Parking my opinion until I've read the details.
I help prepare site-plan applications. The reference numbers tell me where to look, but not what I'd quote a client. Need the actual fee review.
Reviewing the application schedule seems sensible. My support is for updating it appropriately, rather than an assumption that any particular amount is going up or down.
I care about new housing, but the notice doesn't show what the fee change actually is. Neutral on this one.
Not comfortable endorsing an update without the amounts alongside it. We need to be able to plan application costs.
is this more, less, or just organised differently? cant tell from what's here
Yes to maintaining a considered site-plan fee schedule. Review costs deserve attention alongside the rest of the development process.
Working with applications, I'd welcome a schedule that's kept under review. No claim here that it makes my next job cheaper.
Outside my experience. I would need a plain-language explanation of 80 to 84.1.
The proposal is too hard to evaluate from this notice. I'd prefer the comparison with current charges to be front and centre.
My vote is against signing off on an unspecified fee update. Reference numbers aren't an explanation.
An updated schedule isn't automatically good or bad for an applicant. Depends what's in it.
Wondering how the review balances processing costs and encouraging applications. The summary doesn't settle that for me, and I don't want to guess the direction of the change.
I live around Sheppard and would need the parcel drawing to place these two pieces. The street numbers alone don't tell me whether this affects anything I use.
Selling small lane pieces to an adjacent owner sounds practical. Agree that Council should deal with permanent closure first.
I use the area regularly and am wary of permanently closing lane land. I'm unsure about the sale on its own until I understand the footprint.
Having closure approval as a prerequisite makes sense. I don't have a view on inviting this particular purchase.
I'd prefer the City to retain the land. If a sale is considered, requiring Council to approve closure is at least the right order.
What happens to any servicing access? I'm asking, not saying this lane is used for deliveries.
Every tiny bit of city land apparently needs a buyer. I'd keep these pieces too.
Couldn't identify the lane bits from the addresses. No strong view on who buys them.
Two small portions, rather than all of Sheppard. On that understanding I'm comfortable with this going through the closure and sale process.
An adjacent owner is a logical person to invite an offer from. Less sure about the closure question because I don't know the current access arrangement.
Seems a reasonable way to handle surplus pieces. Would like the plan easy to find so neighbours can see exactly what is involved, without guessing at a future building.
I visit the library. A small transfer to the City seems fine to me; this notice doesn't say the library is closing.
32.6 square metres, staying with the City. Mostly sounds administrative.
Municipal purposes is quite open-ended. I'd like to know what use is intended before forming a view.
I'd rather leave the parcel with the library for now. Small bits of land can still be useful, even though I can't point to a particular use for this one.
No objection to moving a surplus parcel between municipal bodies. Doesn't sound like something that needs to be more complicated.
where is the little piece on the library site? Hard to picture 350 square feet from the address
Yes, let the City make use of land the library has declared surplus. Happy with a municipal transfer in principle.
Nothing here changes my view of visiting the library. I'll leave the property details to people who know the parcel.
I'm nearby and comfortable with the proposed sale to 2-Spirited People of the First Nations. I don't know what their plans are, so I'm not treating a particular use as promised.
Would like to see how the sale is being evaluated, including the terms. Naming a buyer isn't the whole decision for me.
I work along Woodbine. No objection to the named purchaser buying the surplus piece; any later use would need its own explanation.
Generally prefer the City to hold onto land. That's why I'm against this disposal, regardless of who the purchaser is.
Pass this area but don't know the property well enough to have much to add.
Glad to see this organisation considered as a purchaser. Support the sale in principle, while leaving space for proper review of whatever terms are proposed.
213.5 m2 is more than a sliver. A parcel plan and explanation would help me work out what I'm looking at.
Not ready to back disposal with no price in the notice. I ask the same question about any buyer of city land.
Sounds reasonable. No specific future use mentioned, so I'll keep my vote to the sale that's actually proposed.
I'd hoard every scrap of public land if it were up to me. Once sold, it's sold.
Could see arguments either way. Surplus status alone doesn't explain the trade-off, but the notice also gives me no basis to claim a bad deal.
Fine with inviting the offer. Please keep the eventual decision easy for neighbours to follow; there is a lot people can imagine from one short property notice.
